def:
Identify Controller field giving the maximum number of Asynchronous Event Request commands the controller accepts outstanding at once, as a 0's based value. Submitting more fails with Asynchronous Event Request Limit Exceeded.
Common confusion: reading it as 1's based and keeping one AER fewer, or one more, than allowed.

Feature 0Bh: the set of event conditions (each SMART / Health critical warning and several notice types) for which the controller completes an outstanding Asynchronous Event Request. A condition that is not enabled is still visible in its log page but produces no event. Revert to defaults after a reset unless saved.
Common confusion: assuming the driver enables SMART warning events.

On a zoned namespace, the host's process of reclaiming space: choose a Full victim zone, copy its live data to another zone (often with Zone Append), make the new mapping durable, then Reset Zone. Host write amplification is 1/(1−u) for victims with live fraction u.
Common confusion: believing ZNS removes write amplification rather than moving it to the host.

A ZNS controller moving an implicitly opened zone to Closed on its own so that it can open another zone within the Maximum Open Resources limit. It returns no error but costs internal work (flushing buffers and parity), so writing round-robin across more zones than the open limit degrades throughput. Which zone is closed is implementation-dependent.
Common confusion: thinking a Closed zone no longer counts as active.

ZNS log page (identifier BFh as encoded in libnvme; confirm in ZNS 1.5) listing zones whose descriptors changed, for example when Finish Zone Recommended or Reset Zone Recommended is set. It accompanies the Zone Descriptor Changed asynchronous event; reading it with RAE cleared re-arms the event.
Common confusion: re-reporting every zone instead of the listed ones.

A host convention, not part of NVMe: a header that a KV library stores inside each value, such as the full application name, a mapping version and a checksum. It lets the library detect hash collisions and migrate key mappings, and it counts toward the value size limit.
Common confusion: forgetting its bytes when checking a value against the maximum value length.
